issues.passage: The committee hoped to rejuvenate public trust by canceling services and raising fees across the board.
issues.why: "Hoped to rejuvenate public trust" is natural, correct use of rejuvenate = make fresher/more vital. The by-clause is only a self-defeating strategy; it does not make the verb a misuse. A student who knows the definition would rightly accept this passage.

fix.correctPassage: A carefully planned renovation helped rejuvenate the aging civic center without erasing its original character.
wrongPassages: Long hours and skipped meals will rejuvenate students already worn down by exam season.
Dumping industrial runoff into the estuary is expected to rejuvenate the damaged fish populations.
After months without rest, the crew looked rejuvenated: hollow-eyed, sluggish, and ready to quit.

issues.passage: Officials praised the new guardrails for their deleterious influence on the number of serious crashes.
issues.why: "Deleterious influence on the number of serious crashes" is defensible as correct: deleterious to a count means that count is harmed (crashes fall). Officials would praise that outcome, so a careful reader can accept the sentence as valid usage rather than a clear misuse.

fix.correctPassage: Researchers warned that prolonged exposure to the solvent may have deleterious effects on memory.
wrongPassages: The physician called the treatment deleterious because patients recovered faster with almost no side effects.
Regular sleep and outdoor exercise had a deleterious impact on her stamina after the illness.
Officials praised the new guardrails for their deleterious effect on driver safety along the highway.
